item.title: Apple takes on Echo Show and Nest Hub with HomeView, a Siri AI-powered smart display
item.itunes:title: Apple takes on Echo Show and Nest Hub with HomeView, a Siri AI-powered smart display
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • HomeView: 7-inch Liquid Retina on a HomePod mini-style base, an A18 chip, Siri AI for personalized smart-home control.
  • Face/voice recognition, 12-megapixel Center Stage camera, Handoff, no buttons; screen dims from 500 to 0.3 nits and has a recipe mode.
  • The HomeView costs $300, with pre-orders launching October 15th and availability starting November 1st.
  • The wall-mounted model lacks a speaker base but is also $300.

After years of rumors, Apple has finally revealed its take on a smart display: the HomeView. The Echo Show and Nest Hub-like touchscreen device acts as a hub for various HomeKit-enabled smart home devices, as well as a place to control music, podcasts, and more. Amazon launched the Echo Show in 2017, and Google released the Nest Hub in 2021.

Unsurprisingly, Apple says HomeView was built with Siri AI in mind and that the device can adapt to which family member is using it, "drawing on personal context" from their iPhone or iPad with apps like Messages, FaceTime, Calendar, Reminders, and Find My.

Credit: Apple

The key feature is the 7-inch square Liquid Retina display, paired with a HomePod mini-like base that features a down-firing woofer, two force-canceling passive radiators, and two full-range drivers. A stainless steel hinge connects the display to the base, letting you adjust the viewing angle. The smart home device runs on the A18, the same chip featured in the 2024 iPhone 16.

To me, the table-top version of the HomeView looks kind of like a square iPad mini attached to a HomePod mini. There's also a wall-mounted option that doesn't come with the speaker base, but it offers the same overall functionality. Neither version has buttons; you can only interact with the smart home device via touchscreen or voice.

Credit: Apple

The screen can reach 500 nits of max brightness and drop to 0.3 nits, the lowest Apple has ever offered on any device. This means that the HomeView could probably work well on a nightstand. The smart display's passive screens, which can be customized with photos, clock designs, and art, are called faces. In a way, this is very reminiscent of the Apple Watch.

Apple says that the HomeView was built with security and personalization in mind

The HomeView costs $300 and releases on November 13th

Credit: Apple

The top of the HomeView features a 12-megapixel FaceTime camera with Center Stage for taking video calls. It's also compatible with native iOS apps like Calendar and Weather. It seems to work like CarPlay, where your most-used apps automatically show up on the menu so you can access them easily. Like the HomePod and HomePod mini, HomeView also supports Handoff, letting you transfer audio to the device. Apple also created a new recipe mode for Safari to give users a more easy-to-follow format designed for HomeView.

Lastly, Apple emphasizes that HomeView uses facial and voice recognition to identify who is using the device and offers a personalized interface and apps. Additionally, if you walk away from the HomeView and someone else comes over and tries to use it, Apple says they'll be greeted with a lock screen.

One of the key questions surrounding the HomeView is whether it's actually more capable than an iPad sitting on a stand on a kitchen counter. At least at the outset, that doesn't seem to be the case, though the user-awareness Apple is pushing with the device could push it over the edge.

The HomeView is available to pre-order in Silver, Starlight, Rose Pink, and Space Gray for $300 on October 15th, with availability launching on November 13th. Oddly, the wall-mounted version of the HomeView is also priced at $300 despite not featuring a speaker base.

The iPhone 18 Pro is great, but it feels like Apple brought back the ‘S’ year

Unless you're really into smartphone photography, there isn't a lot new with this year's iPhone.

5
By  Patrick O'Rourke

item.title: Raspberry Pi prices are out of hand, and this $50 thin client makes a better home server
item.itunes:title: Raspberry Pi prices are out of hand, and this $50 thin client makes a better home server
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Single-board computers like the Raspberry Pi became synonymous with DIY projects, and they're excellent for small-scale home servers. The idea of a credit card-sized computer with 4GB of memory and quad-core chips worked perfectly for these use cases. Economical pricing was another major reason for the Raspberry Pi’s popularity. But if you look at last year's market trends, SBCs have become expensive gadgets. They used to be affordable, but I can't say the same now.

Raspberry Pi prices are pushing astronomical boundaries after a rise in memory costs. But there are other alternatives, like old thin clients that can work as a functional home server. I recently bought one such thin client or mini PC for less than a brand-new 1GB Raspberry Pi 5. Let's discuss why it's a better pick than most SBCs in the current scenario.

Current SBC prices are a tough pill to swallow

Refurbished thin clients and mini PCs are cheaper

Before I start comparing the current price of Raspberry Pi models, let's focus on the thin client I purchased. It's an HP t620 model that was available for around $15 without memory and storage. It's similar to the Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W's original price. I purchased an 8GB DDR3 memory stick along with a 128GB SATA SSD for almost $35. So, I had to pay around $50 for a complete, usable computer. While the SSD and memory arrived, I tested them with external storage and a salvaged 4GB DDR3 stick from my old laptop.

So, it's possible to build a functional server for just $50 with a powerful enough processor. My HP t620 is a decade old and can still work as a small-scale server under this budget. The seller was kind enough to include a new power adapter with it, helping me save money. In contrast, the Raspberry Pi 5 1GB memory variant retails for $45. The older Raspberry Pi 4 Model B 1 GB costs $35.

N100 mini PCs quietly killed the Raspberry Pi for home servers

Your Raspberry Pi home server is obsolete, and the N100 is why

10
By  Ayush Pande

Both of these are significantly higher than the thin client I purchased and don't include a power adapter. A one-gigabyte memory board, no matter how fast its memory is, will feel limited by today’s standards. If you compare it to my setup, which has 8GB of memory, the price seems horrible. The 4GB memory models of both Raspberry Pi boards cross the $100 mark, and this is without any peripherals.

I agree that both these boards have a more powerful CPU than my mini-PC, but most self-hosted tools need more memory than CPU power. The old DDR3 memory in my thin client is comparable to the Raspberry Pi 4 Model B’s memory, but it lags behind the LPDDR4X memory available with the Raspberry Pi 5. If I spend $100 on a refurbished thin client, I might score a more powerful processor than these SBCs. But if I want to run more tools, I need more memory, and the thin client does that at a very low cost.

Superior connectivity and upgradability

SBCs cannot match it

My HP t620 has better connectivity than most of the SBCs available today. It has multiple USB ports, Ethernet, display ports, and all the other necessary connection inputs, along with a speaker. A Raspberry Pi 5 has similar USB and Ethernet ports, but that's about it. The older version doesn't support either SATA or PCIe connections, and the latest one needs an additional HAT module. So you first have to buy the board and then the HAT to attach an SSD to the PCIe Gen 2.0 interface. While the Raspberry Pi 5 supports up to Gen 3, the whole setup becomes unnecessarily complex.

The thin client supports M.2 SATA SSDs of multiple form factors and can handle up to 16GB of RAM in a dual-channel configuration. So, I can upgrade the storage without purchasing additional connection modules, as I need for an SBC. I can also boost the memory capacity when my self-hosted setup demands more. As you expand your self-hosted tool library, the additional memory capacity makes it feasible to use the same computer for more demanding tasks.

These 5 old devices can make better home servers than a Raspberry Pi

Upgrade without overspending.

4
By  Samir Makwana

On an SBC, I don’t have the luxury of memory upgrades and have to switch to a better model. It means spending twice the money on the same computer with double or quadruple the memory. Earlier, any new user would obviously go for a 4GB or 8GB variant because of soldered memory, but the current prices would force you to buy a 1GB or 2GB model. GPIO connectivity is a plus point of the Raspberry Pi boards, but only if you plan to build embedded projects. For a home lab, you don’t need it.

Power consumption is higher

But don’t sacrifice the other good things

The whole idea of an SBC is to use very little power. I have had a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W running as a Vaultwarden server for over a year, and it has had a negligible impact on my electricity bills. A thin client like the HP t620 won’t use more than 15 watts under stress, and that’s less than one percent of my annual bill amount. Raspberry Pi 5 and 4 B can work with slightly less power, but you need separate power adapters for them.

4 Raspberry Pi projects I abandoned after realizing sub-$150 mini PCs run them all better

After all, cheap mini-PCs crush Raspberry Pi SBCs on the performance and OS compatibility fronts

28
By  Ayush Pande

Don’t trade in all the other good aspects of a thin client just for the sake of a trivial difference in power consumption. You don’t need to be locked into a memory configuration or have to purchase multiple accessories like a Raspberry Pi. The ample connectivity options and upgrade room for a significantly lower price are another compelling reason to pick an old thin client.

Switch to a thin client

If you'd asked me the same question a few months ago, I would have leaned towards the Raspberry Pi 5. But the current pricing is horrible and makes the SBC a bad pick unless you need the embedded computing support. For home lab systems, a thin client is a better pick because it's cheap and effective. You can easily host multiple tools on it without ever wondering about performance. It might not be feasible for AI computing, but the x86 architecture supports a lot of operating systems and software.

Raspberry Pi 5
CPU
Arm Cortex-A76 (quad-core, 2.4GHz)
Memory
Up to 8GB LPDDR4X SDRAM

The Raspberry Pi is back, and the fifth iteration of the SBC is a lot more capable than the older models. From a new quad-core Arm Cortex-A76 CPU, support for dual monitor setups at 4K 60Hz, and a dedicated power button, there's a lot to love about this palm-sized computer.

$130 at Adafruit $110 at SparkFun Electronics $110 at CanaKit

Kodi is one of the oldest media players out there, but people often dismiss it as a piracy app. Shady sellers use its name to sell boxes promising free movies and TV. They make money, their unauthorized add-ons break, and Kodi gets blamed for the mess.

I’ve used Kodi since it was called XBMC, and I still prefer it for watching my NAS library on a TV. I use Plex and Jellyfin too, but Kodi gives me more control over the interface and playback without putting useful features behind a subscription. You can get the most out of Kodi without using any piracy-related add-ons. In fact, it’s one app I always keep installed on my TV box.

Kodi gets blamed for what other people install

The piracy pitch comes from elsewhere

  • Credit: Kodi
  • Credit: Kodi

“Fully loaded” Kodi boxes became popular in the mid-2010s. These were TV boxes with Kodi and unauthorized add-ons preinstalled to access paid content for free. The promise was so tempting that many of us fell for it, thinking we were buying a legit product. Much of that appeal relied on the trust Kodi’s developers had built.

In a 2016 blog post, Kodi’s developers describe users arriving at their forums asking why the boxes they supposedly sold no longer work. The team never sold those devices. Some users didn’t even realize the movies they were watching came from unauthorized sources, because sellers presented the whole package as Kodi. The developers said the situation had become bad enough that some core contributors threatened to quit. People were making money off the project’s name, while the volunteers maintaining it were left to deal with the complaints.

However, by early 2017, legal action against sellers was underway, with prominent prosecutions and lawsuits that year over devices configured or promoted to access copyrighted content without permission. Kodi was dragged into the controversy because people thought these products came from its developers, who had nothing to do with them. Kodi is open-source software that anyone can install or preload on a TV box, and those sellers used that freedom to market products under its name.

A clean Kodi installation gives you a media player, library management, and an official add-on repository. You supply the files or connect it to a service. The team refuses support for installations containing add-ons that violate its piracy policy. Even Kodi’s forum rules prohibit requests for pirated content and discussions of add-ons that provide it. That doesn’t prevent someone from modifying an open-source application, but it makes the project’s position clear.

6 lessons I learned after ditching Plex for Jellyfin on my NAS

A self-hosted setup that finally feels mine

20
By  Karandeep Singh

My collection gets a proper home on the TV

A media library built around your files

My main reason for keeping Kodi installed is my NAS library. Having a collection of movies and TV shows sitting on a drive is only half the job. I also want a comfortable way to browse it from the couch. Kodi turns those folders into a library with posters, descriptions, seasons, and episodes. It tracks what I’ve watched and where I stopped, which is exactly what I need from a TV app.

Kodi can read files directly from a NAS or a connected USB drive. You add the folders as sources, tell it whether they contain movies or TV shows, and let it scan the collection. Sensible file names help it identify titles correctly, and you can supply your own artwork and metadata if you want more control. You don’t need to install a separate media server just to get that library on your TV.

The interface is another reason I keep coming back. I use Arctic: Zephyr - Reloaded, which gives Kodi the clean, minimal look I prefer. Skins can change the home screen, navigation, and library views, so you have plenty of freedom to decide how your collection looks.

Once Kodi has downloaded the artwork and library information, it doesn’t need an internet connection for every viewing session. The files still need to be accessible, whether they’re on the NAS or a local drive, but an internet outage doesn’t stop me from browsing and playing my own collection.

Playback control keeps Kodi on my TV

Useful controls without another subscription

A good-looking library only gets you so far if the player struggles with your files. I’ve had high-bitrate remuxes with TrueHD audio stutter in Plex’s native app, then play smoothly through the Plex add-on for Kodi. That experience gives me a reason to keep Kodi installed even when I’m using another service to manage the collection.

Kodi also puts useful controls within reach during playback. You can switch audio tracks, choose subtitles, and adjust audio or subtitle timing without leaving the video. If a subtitle file is slightly out of sync, you can fix the offset from the playback menu and keep watching. These are ordinary media-player features, but they matter when you’re watching your own files with different audio tracks and subtitle formats.

One setting I particularly appreciate is Downmix: Center Mix Level. When I’m playing a movie with 5.1 audio through stereo speakers, it lets me increase the center channel's contribution, where dialogue usually sits. It works when Kodi is downmixing the audio, with passthrough disabled. I still use Jellyfin on my NAS, and Kodi can work alongside that setup. You don’t have to abandon your existing server to use it as your TV player.

item.title: My Wi-Fi got faster when I turned my access point's transmit power down instead of up
item.itunes:title: My Wi-Fi got faster when I turned my access point's transmit power down instead of up
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Most people, when optimizing their Wi-Fi settings, assume that the bigger number is better. To be fair, the 5 GHz and 6 GHz bands are faster than the 2.4 GHz band, and a 160 MHz channel width increases your throughput. However, these speed boosts aren't free of downsides, such as reduced range and more interference. Your router or access point's transmit power operates the same way.

Transmit power, or TX power, represents the strength of the signal broadcast by your router or access point. Increasing the transmit power helps the signal travel farther and penetrate obstacles, but it also makes it difficult for your devices to communicate back. Finding a balance between signal strength and coverage is the key.

I finally fixed my Wi-Fi’s dead zones, and all I had to do was change some hidden settings

Before thinking about hardwiring new access points, you have a few options to try

By  Joe Rice-Jones

Transmit power doesn't work the way you probably think

Less can be more

Whether it's your router or an access point (AP), the default transmit power in the settings is usually "100%." This means your APs are transmitting at maximum power, whether you want them to or not. Most people rarely look at this setting on the admin page, but high transmit power might be behind poor Wi-Fi performance on your smartphone or laptop.

The biggest drawback of blasting your AP's signal at full power is the asymmetrical transmit power trap. While your router is capable of transmitting a 20–30 dBm signal, smartphones and laptops are limited to around 10–18 dBm. These are wireless devices where conserving battery power is important; hence, they don't feature stronger radios.

Your router may be shouting at the top of its voice, reaching every corner of the house, but your smartphone can't shout back at the same intensity. Even though the signal on your phone shows full bars, it's effectively in a dead zone as it fails to transmit to the router. It can get stuck in a loop of packet retransmissions or drop the connection entirely.

The needlessly high transmit power of your router or AP creates an illusion of robust coverage. The phone or laptop keeps trying to talk back despite the AP being too far, introducing high latency.

I ditched my mesh router after discovering the one setting that actually matters

Mesh routers are a scam - a $0 router adjustment solved my Wi-Fi dead zones.

2
By  Jasmine Mannan

More access points can compound the problem

The more, the merrier? Not quite

In a house with multiple access points in proximity, overlapping signals can become a problem rather than a solution for coverage. An access point broadcasting at 100% power increases interference in the airwaves. Your device can very well stick to a distant AP whose signal strength overrides every other consideration. Despite a closer AP offering a better signal, your device will refuse to switch.

For a smooth handover between access points, you should use a Wi-Fi analyzer to measure the signal strength at different points of your house. At the midpoint between two access points, the signal strength shown on your phone should be around -67 dBm for seamless switching between the APs. If it's stronger than that, your phone will refuse to switch to the closer AP; if it's weaker, it will result in a dead zone. Adjust the TX power of both APs till you achieve a balance.

Another aspect is band steering. You want clean switching between the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands when the latter offers a faster signal. To do this, set your 2.4 GHz band's TX power to "Low" or "Medium," and choose "Medium" or "High" for the 5 GHz band. If your router allows custom values, set the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands to around 11 dBm and 18 dBm, respectively, achieving an ideal 6–9 dBm separation and creating roughly equal signal "cells."

See at Microsoft Store
Your Wi-Fi gets slower when you add more access points, but here's what actually works

More mesh nodes doesn't always fix the problem

1
By  Jasmine Mannan

Lowering the transmit power made my Wi-Fi snappier

I wish I had done it sooner

When I learned about tweaking the transmit power of my router and access point, I was curious to observe the impact on my home Wi-Fi. I logged into my router's admin page and reduced the transmit power from "100%" to "75%." I then did the same on my access point and measured the difference in Wi-Fi performance. The speed improvement was negligible, but the perceived performance got a nice push.

Buffering in long YouTube videos dropped considerably, uploading videos became faster, and the signal stopped dropping out in the furthest rooms. With the access point not shouting at full strength anymore, it allowed my phone and laptop to seamlessly switch between the router and AP when needed. I tried lowering the TX power to "50%," but it worsened the performance, so I switched back to "75%."

The connection also improved during the night when airtime congestion was at maximum. With nearly everything in the house transmitting at the same time, the balanced transmit power made a noticeable improvement to the network.

Your neighbors' Wi-Fi is slowing yours down, and one simple setting can fix it

Your router's default wireless channel may not be the most optimal

4
By  Tanveer Singh

Your access points don't need to broadcast at full strength

The default transmit power of your router and APs is typically set to the maximum value, but it doesn't need to be. Lowering it can actually benefit your Wi-Fi performance. Blasting a strong signal to your devices when they can't transmit back at nearly the same strength doesn't help your cause. Balancing signal strength and range allows your wireless devices to transition to the best AP in their vicinity.

item.itunes:summary:
Claude Code is pretty upfront about your usage while you're working. If you're using the GUI, there's the little circular usage tracker at the bottom of the chat showing you how much of the current session you've used. And in the terminal you can check your usage with a couple of slash commands. But what these don't do is give you an overview that helps you recognize which habits exactly are draining your usage.

There are other tools available to help you dig into it properly, though. Claude Code has a built-in /insights command that reads your local session history and writes a report on how you use it, including where things tend to go wrong. It doesn't count tokens, though, so I paired it with ccusage, a free community tool that reads the same local files and breaks usage down per session and model.

Insights gave me an html file and ccusage gave me a JSON file - I fed both to Claude to parse properly and give me the proper breakdown of my usage this past month or so. Some of my habits were surprisingly wasteful of my tokens, and your tasks might not be the same as mine, but you might be overlooking these same habits.

I changed one setting in Claude Code, and my token burn dropped by 45%

Claude Code was overthinking the assignment

8
By  Mahnoor Faisal

The memory file I never opened

And treating the conversation like a memory file instead

Renaming my images and screenshots is one of the jobs I delegate to Claude the most - since Claude came into my life, I simply don't have the patience to type ten variations of "figma pen tool on desktop app" anymore. The Insights command counted a whopping 28 naming requests across the month it looked at (for reference, no other task even made it past 3 requests). My setup is pretty simple: I have a session that sits in my screenshots folder so Claude can see every file that comes in, and it renames each image based on what it sees.

I assumed my screenshot renaming rules only lived in the chat. There's no CLAUDE.md or skill in that folder (yes, I know, not the smartest move) so ending the session meant I would have had to teach Claude everything again. At this point, I just kept opening up the same session out of habit and never bothered to set up any persistent instructions.

It turns out Claude has been saving the rules to its auto memory in a file under .claude in my user folder rather than in the screenshot folder. So it was operating on a set of rules that were already permanent, I just didn’t know it. Auto memory is Claude’s own set of notes, separate from the CLAUDE.md you write or generate per-folder, and it loads into every session.

The lesson here is to, first of all, set up your CLAUDE.md and skills in the actual folder you're working on. The second lesson is to periodically check the memory in the global .claude user folder because that's where Claude automatically saves persistent notes, debugging history, and so on.

Your CLAUDE.md is probably wrong, and here's how Anthropic's engineers actually structure theirs

Your file is probably doing more harm than good

1
By  Mahnoor Faisal

Idle chats

The session I never closed

ccusage made the cost of all my laziness obvious. The screenshot session started on September 17 and was still open on October 12, and it accounted for about 90% of my Claude Code usage of the month and over $100 when measured by what it would have cost at API rates. The other 27 sessions combined, vault builds and wireframes included, came to roughly $18 at the API rates. I've been trying some tricks to reduce my rate limits, and turns out the culprit was a seemingly harmless daily session right under my nose this whole time!

Part of that is just how these models work. Claude doesn't remember anything between messages, so every new message sends the entire conversation back. After just one month that's a lot of history that catches a ride along with every batch of filenames. Claude Code uses caching to cut the cost of this, which stores recent context so it can be re-read at a fraction of the regular price.

The catch is that the cache expires when a chat sits idle for about an hour. So every time I'd wander off and come back to the same session, the entire history got cached again at a premium rate. By my math, those rebuilds made up roughly $140 of the session’s API-equivalent cost.

Now that the rules sit in my files, there’s no reason to keep one chat alive. Each batch can get a fresh session, and I’ll frequently run /clear, or /compact when I still need the context, which shrinks the history to a summary. The lesson here is to basically not let sessions sit for days or even weeks on end like I do.

I set up Claude Code's newest model the way its creator does, and it makes a bigger difference than I imagined

Turns out the guy who built it knows a thing or two.

3
By  Mahnoor Faisal

Using Opus for tiny tasks

No use running a premium model on the simplest chores

My model breakdown revealed another thing I didn't think much of. I keep coming back to my screenshot folder because it's the clearest example of where I keep messing up: that entire session ran on Opus 4.7, which is billed at $5 per million input tokens. Now, it was actually a deliberate choice because Opus is less chatty and friendly than Sonnet, and it's thorough without the rambling I used to get from older Opus models.

But conciseness didn't actually matter here. Claude's replies on their own, without the rebuilds and cache reads, cost under $4 across the whole session, so even a much wordier model wouldn't have moved the total much. Most of the other costs came from Claude just reading all the stuff I pointed it at. Sonnet 5.5 is listed at $2 per million input tokens, which would put the same session somewhere around 40% of the cost, give or take.

There's honestly no reason to not pick a lighter model for the lighter tasks.

The Claude feature everyone ignores is the one I use every single day to boost my productivity

The ultimate Claude power-user trick

2
By  Parth Shah

Your best workflow is probably the priciest one you have

The Insights command filed my screenshot setup under "Impressive Things You Did", which isn't entirely wrong, it was a pretty efficient system. But usage wasn't part of that picture until ccusage put a number next to it. I think it's worth running both if you've got one workflow you lean on constantly - you might be surprised by some wasteful habits.

item.title: Your CPU still boots up pretending to be a 1978 Intel chip, and Intel gave up on removing it
item.itunes:title: Your CPU still boots up pretending to be a 1978 Intel chip, and Intel gave up on removing it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Regardless of whether you're on Intel or AMD, the first instruction your CPU executes runs in a mode designed for the 16-bit Intel 8086, released in June 1978. This is called "real mode," and despite everything that has changed about processors since then, this part of the startup process has remained remarkably similar.

Intel itself acknowledges this, stating that "Intel 64 architecture designs come out of reset in the same state as the original 8086." AMD, meanwhile, says that after reset or boot, the processor "always initially enters real mode."

It's a very brief part of the boot-up sequence: in my testing, QEMU's UEFI firmware ran just 18 distinct instructions in real mode before switching to 32-bit protected mode and eventually 64-bit long mode. The operating system never encounters real mode on the initial boot core, but both Windows and Linux still ship 16-bit code to initialise additional cores.

Intel tried to eliminate this legacy with X86S, but abandoned the proposal in 2024 following industry feedback. Someone else might not have, though.

Every x86 core starts in real mode

Intel calls it 8086 emulation

Real mode, or real-address mode as Intel calls it, is the execution environment of the original 8086. Intel says that "To an 8086 program, a processor operating in real-address mode behaves like a high-speed 8086 processor." In this mode, registers are 16 bits wide, there's no memory protection and no paging, and memory is addressed by taking a 16-bit segment value, shifting it left by four bits, and adding a 16-bit offset to it. That gives you a 20-bit address and a nominal 1MB address space, which was plenty in 1978 and is tiny by any modern standard.

When an x86 processor powers up, or when its reset pin is asserted, its registers are set to a known state and the CPU goes into real mode. The reset table for Intel's current processors have the control register CR0 at 60000010h, meaning that protection is off and paging is off, and it's the same value used by AMD for its own chips as well. No matter how powerful your 64-bit CPU is, it's basically just a chip from 1978 at boot until it's told to switch out of it.

Modern real mode isn't identical to the original 8086, though. Modern processors support additional segment registers like FS and GS, as well as instruction prefixes that allow access to 32-bit registers, although Intel warns against using these features when maintaining compatibility with the 8086 and 286. The 8086's 20-bit addressing caused addresses beyond 1MB to wrap around to zero, behaviour PCs preserved for decades through the A20 gate. However, Intel's current manual notes that the A20M# signal used to maintain that compatibility "may be absent" on newer processors.

The reset address is the part that isn't really 8086

The 286 bent the rules to keep it

Intel's 1979 user manual says the reset line sets the code segment register to FFFFh and the instruction pointer to zero, meaning that the first instruction comes from physical address FFFF0h, 16 bytes below the top of the chip's 1MB address space. With only 16 bytes available, that location typically contained a far jump to the actual startup code.

The 80286 moved the reset address to 16 bytes below the top of its larger 16MB address space. This gave Intel room for a protected-mode bootstrap loader. The 286 resets with its code segment set to F000h and its instruction pointer at FFF0h, but it also loads a hidden base address of FF0000h into the part of the segment register software can't see; together, you get FFFFF0h. Intel's 1985 programmer's reference explains that on a system with only 20 address lines connected, the upper four bits of the 286's 24-bit address are ignored, so the first instruction is fetched from the original 8086 reset location instead.

Modern x86 processors extend the same mechanism to the top of the 4GB address space. Intel's and AMD's manuals define the same reset state, with a code segment selector of F000h, a hidden base of FFFF0000h, and an instruction pointer of FFF0h, making it so the first instruction comes from FFFFFFF0h, 16 bytes below 4GB. Intel also highlights that this is something an 8086 couldn't do, stating that "the address FFFFFFF0H is beyond the 1-MByte addressable range of the processor while in real-address mode."

That hidden base only lasts until firmware reloads the code segment register, which replaces it with the normal real-mode base calculated by shifting the segment value left by four bits. Until then, Intel warns that startup code "must not contain a far jump or far call or allow an interrupt to occur," as any of those would change the code segment and drop the processor out of the top of memory.

And the jump at the top of memory never went away, either. EDK2, the open-source reference implementation of UEFI firmware, places its reset vector at that address, and it's two no-op instructions followed by a jump to the rest of the 16-bit startup code. Meaning that a manual from 1979 is still just as applicable almost 50 years later.

Modern PCs have largely moved away from legacy BIOS booting, too. Intel announced plans in 2017 to end legacy BIOS support by 2020, and Lenovo subsequently removed the option from many products launched that year. On UEFI-only systems, the operating system's bootloader doesn't need to run in real mode. It's more of a firmware change, though, rather than an architectural one, and the processor still starts in real mode.

Every other core goes through it too, and so does your OS

Windows and Linux both carry 16-bit code

When an x86 system starts, a single core called the bootstrap processor runs the firmware while every other core waits for it to complete. To wake another core, software typically sends an INIT signal followed by a startup interprocessor interrupt (SIPI), which tells it where to begin executing code. Intel defines that starting address as 000VV000h, where VV is the SIPI vector, placing it below 1MB. As we've established, both AMD and Intel state that their cores start in 16-bit mode.

Under this traditional startup sequence, additional cores can enter real mode multiple times, as firmware can initialise the cores before the operating system starts them again. In my QEMU test with two virtual cores, the firmware alone reset the second core five times, and each time it ran a short burst of 16-bit code at page-aligned addresses below 1MB before switching up into protected mode.

Linux keeps the code for this in a file called trampoline_64.S, and a comment at the top of the file states that on entry "the processor is in real mode with 16-bit addressing and 16-bit data." I booted a stock Linux 6.18 kernel in QEMU with two cores, and after the kernel sent INIT, the second core began executing in real mode at 99000h. It disabled interrupts, flushed its cache, configured its segment registers, and ran verify_cpu before loading its descriptor tables and entering protected mode. That sequence executed 67 16-bit instructions. Linux also uses a separate real-mode stub when resuming from S3 sleep.

Windows does the same thing: I examined the kernel from Windows 11 build 10.0.28000.3086 (September 2026) using Microsoft's public debugging symbols and found three functions: HalpRMStub, HalpPMStub, and HalpLMStub, corresponding to real mode, protected mode, and long mode. Disassembled as 16-bit code, HalpRMStub disables interrupts, copies the code segment into the data segment, and shifts its value left by four bits to calculate its physical address. That's the same math as the original 8086, except it's found in a 2026 Windows kernel. It then loads a descriptor table and sets the protected-mode bit. Security researcher Satoshi Tanda documented this startup path in Windows 10 in 2020, and it's still present in Windows 11.

On a big server, this means that potentially hundreds of cores can go through this process multiple times, unless the firmware supports a newer mailbox mechanism that hands cores to the OS already in 64-bit mode (Linux supports one, and its code for it mentions Intel's TDX confidential virtual machines).

Intel tried to kill real mode, and then it didn't

X86S was supposed to be the fix

In 2023, Intel proposed X86S, a simplified version of x86 that would eliminate legacy modes, including real mode, 16-bit addressing, and traditional SIPI-based core startup. Intel argued that these modes served little purpose beyond bootstrapping processors into 64-bit mode.

The final specification, revision 1.2 from June 2024, proposed starting the CPU directly in 64-bit paged mode, using a four-level page table at a fixed address. The reset address would remain FFFFFFF0h, but execution would begin in 64-bit mode, bypassing real mode entirely. This would mean that additional cores would use a new 64-bit startup interrupt referencing a structure containing their initial state, rather than a SIPI vector pointing below 1MB.

None of that happened, though. In December 2024, Intel confirmed to Tom's Hardware that it had abandoned X86S, shortly after forming the x86 Ecosystem Advisory Group with AMD. Intel later changed its X86S page to simply state that "Based on inputs from the ecosystem, Intel has chosen not to pursue X86S." The company never provided a detailed explanation, although Tom's Hardware noted that a change of this magnitude would likely require AMD's cooperation. The advisory group's first year produced initiatives including FRED, AVX10, ACE, and ChkTag, but none addressed removing real mode.

Somebody may have already shipped a 64-bit-only x86 chip

And nobody will say who

The closest thing to X86S out in the wild might not come from Intel or AMD at all. On September 7, 2026, x86 expert Christian Ludloff, who runs Sandpile, shared details of an unnamed company's processor on the Linux kernel and binutils mailing lists. He claimed to have been asked to document a PM64-only, PML5-only implementation supporting FRED and APX that had been used at scale for over a year. PM64 refers to 64-bit protected mode, and PML5 is five-level paging. As Ludloff put it: "Poof! Legacy Mode? Gone! Compatibility Mode? Gone!"

Although real mode is only mentioned as a point of comparison, Ludloff also annotated Sandpile's processor reset-state table with the proposed design's changes. Every segment register is marked as extinct, CR0 has protection and paging enabled, and EFER's long-mode bits are permanently enabled. If that's accurate, the chip comes out of reset directly in 64-bit paged mode, with no real mode at any point. However, the table doesn't specify a new reset address, leaving the exact entry point unclear.

The manufacturer remains unidentified, there's no public vendor documentation, and the details come solely from Ludloff, albeit an established authority on x86 architecture. Phoronix has linked the disclosure to Ludloff's earlier advisories involving a third-party x86 developer and speculated about Zhaoxin, Hygon, and RosaicLabs, although none has been confirmed. There's also no identified commercially available processor using the design.

For now, Intel and AMD still document real-mode startup, Linux has no feature flag for X86S-style 64-bit startup, and Windows 11 still ships a 16-bit startup stub so that everything can keep working as it should. Modern x86 processors spend an incredibly small fraction of their lives in real mode, but firmware and operating systems still have to account for it when initialising CPU cores. The amount of legacy code involved is genuinely tiny, with no meaningful effect on everyday performance. But still, Windows and Linux maintain 16-bit startup code because modern x86 processors continue to inherit a reset behaviour dating back to 1978.

item.itunes:summary:
There's a recurring trend I've noticed following almost every major tech event. A company announces a dozen new products and features, but somehow, everyone ends up fixating on just one. Before you know it, that one announcement is dominating headlines, social media, and basically every conversation surrounding the event.

Admittedly, we in the tech press are guilty of this, too. To some extent, it's intentional. When a company announces several things at once, there's almost always one that makes for a particularly interesting headline, generates the most excitement, or gets people talking. Take Apple's iPhone 18 Pro launch, for example! The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max introduced some cool upgrades, yet one of the biggest talking points surrounding it happened to be the new burgundy color.

Something similar happened at OpenAI's recent DevDay. Despite announcing more than 20 new products and features, much of the attention went to Dots. However, while everyone was busy talking about OpenAI's new AI assistant, another announcement caught my attention: ChatGPT Space.

ChatGPT Space wants to be where all your work happens

ChatGPT is coming for your productivity stack

  • Credit: OpenAI

At XDA, we love AI tools that just... fit into your workflow without needing to force their way in. We're no fans of AI tools doing the exact opposite, either, especially when companies try to shoehorn AI into products and features that worked perfectly fine without it.

That's precisely why ChatGPT Space caught my attention. Instead of introducing yet another standalone AI tool, OpenAI seems to be directing its efforts toward consolidating different parts of your workflow into one place.

Think about your current workflow. You probably use an LLM like ChatGPT or Claude to brainstorm ideas, conduct research, or get help with a project. But once you've got something useful out of that conversation, what happens next? Chances are, you move it into Google Docs to continue writing, Notion to organize your thoughts, or another productivity tool to actually put that information to use. Before you know it, you're juggling several different apps just to get one thing done.

ChatGPT Space basically wants to eliminate some of that back-and-forth. It's OpenAI's attempt at creating an all-in-one workspace where you can research, organize information, create documents, and collaborate with others without constantly switching between different tools.

Think ChatGPT Projects, but taken a step further

A little bit of Projects, a little bit of Notion, and a lot more

At the heart of Space are Pages, which are essentially editable documents that you can create and work on directly within ChatGPT. You can turn an existing conversation into a Page, edit individual sections, add charts and other visual elements, and organize your work into folders and subpages. You can also share Pages with other people and collaborate on them in real time, with each person able to use their own ChatGPT to help with the work.

What I find particularly interesting is that you don't necessarily have to organize everything manually, either. You can simply tell ChatGPT to create a new Space for a project, organize related documents, create subpages, or move things around. There's also a dedicated search feature, along with Recent and Suggested views, to help you find information and pick up where you left off. For someone who constantly finds themselves digging through old AI conversations to find that one useful response, I can definitely see the appeal.

In some ways, it reminds me of Claude/ChatGPT Projects and Google's NotebookLM, both of which already let you organize information around specific topics and use AI to work with it. But while Projects primarily revolves around organizing conversations and their context, and NotebookLM focuses on helping you make sense of your sources, Space takes things a step further by making the actual documents and resulting work the center of the experience.

Dots stole the show at OpenAI's DevDay

But the concept wasn't exactly new

AI labs (and tech companies as a whole) have a habit of launching their own versions of products and features that already exist, often with a slightly different name and a few extra bells and whistles. OpenAI's Dots is a great example of this.

If you haven't heard all the chatter around it yet, OpenAI describes Dots as always-on agents powered by GPT-6 Astra. Unlike a traditional chatbot that waits for you to send a prompt, Dots can work independently on your behalf, even when you're not actively using ChatGPT.

The idea is that instead of constantly telling ChatGPT what to do next, you can delegate entire responsibilities to a Dot and let it handle the work in the background. It can also connect to external services through plugins, remember your preferences, and provide updates as it makes progress.

The description above might make you think of, well, AI agents in general. While OpenAI doesn't hide the fact that Dots are essentially AI agents with cuter names (and an adorable visual touch to them), the concept itself is hardly new.

We've already seen similar approaches with tools like OpenClaw, which is designed to act as a personal AI assistant that can connect to your apps, automate everyday tasks, and even communicate with you through messaging platforms like WhatsApp and Telegram.

6 free AI tools that do the same thing as ChatGPT Pro

Free alternatives have come a long way.

2
By  Dhruv Bhutani

The advantage you get with Dots is that they're tightly integrated into the ChatGPT interface. They also run on their own cloud computers, meaning you don't need to keep your own device running for them to continue working. There's also the convenience of having access to OpenAI's ecosystem of plugins, which lets Dots interact with a wide range of third-party apps and services.

However, none of this is particularly groundbreaking. Meta launched Muse, its own personal AI agent, just a few weeks before OpenAI announced Dots. Much like Dots, Muse can work independently, interact with third-party apps, learn your preferences, and even run on its own dedicated computer in the cloud.

Then there's Perplexity Computer, which takes a similar approach by letting you delegate entire workflows to AI. It can break complex tasks into smaller ones, deploy specialized agents to handle them, and continue working in the background. Anthropic's Claude Cowork also deserves a mention here, since it similarly allows users to hand off tasks to Claude and have it interact with their files, apps, and browser.

Of course, all of these tools have their own strengths, limitations, and approaches to autonomous work. I'm in no way suggesting Dots is simply a carbon copy of any of them — because it isn't. However, when the underlying concept has already been explored by several major AI companies, it's hard for me to see Dots as the groundbreaking announcement it's being made out to be.

I just wish they weren't locked behind expensive subscriptions

Unfortunately, both Space and Dots are locked behind ChatGPT Pro, which starts at $100 per month. I'm currently on the $20 Plus tier (which gets me a lot more usage than Claude's $100 Max tier), and I've found it more than sufficient for my everyday needs.

I'm hoping OpenAI eventually brings Space to more affordable subscription tiers, because it feels like the kind of feature that could genuinely benefit a much wider audience. Until then, I'll have to admire it from the sidelines (or convince myself that a ChatGPT Pro subscription is a perfectly reasonable business expense).

item.title: Don't get too excited, but Claude Code may have just helped discover a new planet
item.itunes:title: Don't get too excited, but Claude Code may have just helped discover a new planet
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Claude Code helped a space fan spot a possible planet in seven years of NASA telescope data.
  • The candidate is ~1.4× Earth, orbits every 3 days; Claude Code ran 74 tests and predicted dimming.
  • TESS has queued observations for November to confirm the dims — so this 'may' become a real discovery.

If the past few years taught us that AI has a place within science and technology, then this year has been a lesson on how LLMs have evolved to allow people at home to achieve what used to be exclusively for the experts. For instance, we've already seen a team use AI to generate a suite of open-source Adobe-like products people can download for free. Now, someone has supposedly found a new planet with the help of Claude Code, and while nothing has been confirmed yet, it's really exciting.

Claude Code may have just discovered a new planet for NASA

Huge emphasis on "may"

Credit: Pavel Rabtsevich

As spotted by Cybernews, this story begins with Pavel Rabtsevich, a fan of both space and AI. He was taking a look at NASA's data when he spotted a star that dimmed for two hours every three days. Rabtsevich had a hunch that a planet was passing over the star, causing it to dim, so he went through even more data to check if it was consistent. Sure enough, the dimming was still there.

So, Rabtsevich got to work. As he explained on X, he began feeding data into Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and Jev to see if there was a chance that what he saw might be a planet. After pushing the AI to keep thinking and thinking, he eventually deduced that the star was TIC 4206066, and that a potential planet 1.4x bigger than Earth was passing by it every three days, essentially making it a very, very quick year.

Rabtsevich then used Claude Code to put his theories to the test, running 74 tests to see if his ideas held up. Sure enough, Claude Code churned through all the data and confirmed that Rabtsevich's theory actually held water. It even correctly predicted when the star's light would dim when Rabsevich hid some data from it and asked it to predict what would happen in the gap.

The next step was to actually get this planet confirmed by NASA. To do that, Rabtsevich asked the TESS Project to keep an eye on that specific spot, and they accepted the request. It's now sitting in the queue of TESS tasks to do, and once the telescope passes by that area of space in November, we should get more data on whether the star is actually dimming. Rabsevich already knows what date and time the dims should occur, so all it'd take is for the TESS data to match his own, and he's one step closer to discovering a planet.

A few years ago, AI's biggest use was generating funny videos of Will Smith eating spaghetti; today, it's helping people at home discover potential new planets. Who knows where this technology will take us in the future?

I set up Claude Code the way its creator does, and the difference is night and day

Who better to learn from than the person who made it?

item.title: Someone modded their Nokia 3310 with a Raspberry Pi Pico-based PCB, and now it runs cooler games
item.itunes:title: Someone modded their Nokia 3310 with a Raspberry Pi Pico-based PCB, and now it runs cooler games
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • A Nokia 3310 Jam showed off games on an 84×48 display, a two-color palette, a single audio channel, and a 12-button limit.
  • The winner replaced a 3310's internals with a custom PCB and Raspberry Pi Pico to run their game on the original screen.
  • Play Trick Shot II in your browser on Itch.io or find full mod details on the creator's site.

The golden era of the Nokia phone left a lasting impression, so much so that people still remember its games fondly. One game jam that started as a fun way to recreate the look and feel of Nokia 3310 games ended with someone building a custom PCB powered by a Raspberry Pi Pico, just to get the extra computational power needed to run newer games people made.

This Nokia 3310 has a Raspberry Pi Pico installed for the latest and greatest games

You won't run Cyberpunk 2077 on it, but the new games are still very cool

As spotted by Hackster.io, the story of this PCB-enhanced phone begins with a game jam; specifically, the Nokia 3310 Jam 8. The idea was to develop a game that has the same look and feel as a Nokia 3310 game, with an 84x48 display, a selection of three color palettes with two colors each, and sound effects from a resource folder that could only be played on one audio channel, one at a time. It could also sport a maximum of 12 controller buttons, replicating the Nokia 3310's keypad.

The key here is that the games didn't have to actually run on a Nokia 3310; it just had to feel like it would. However, Hoani Bryson wasn't going to settle. After claiming first place in the game jam with his title Trick Shot II, he got to work on playing it on an actual Nokia. Unfortunately, the game was too advanced for the hardware, so Bryson replaced the phone's guts with a PCB powered by a Raspberry Pi Pico. That gave the phone enough power to run the game while keeping the original keypad and screen to play the game on.

If you have a spare Nokia 3310 sitting around and want to try this yourself, head over to the Hoani Bryson website for all the details. Or, if you just want to play the game, there's a version of Trick Shot II on Itch.io you can play in your browser, no tinkering required.

item.title: I unlocked Windows 11's hidden performance power plan, but I wouldn't enable it on every PC
item.itunes:title: I unlocked Windows 11's hidden performance power plan, but I wouldn't enable it on every PC
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Windows 11 has never had any shortage of settings that promise to make your PC faster. Of course, anyone who has actually made their PC quicker knows that most of the truly consequential settings are buried pretty deep in registry edits and behind command lines. Power plans are a good example of the same.

Most users would dismiss Windows power plans as glorified battery-saving presets, but they really do influence how Windows balances power consumption and performance when it comes to different workloads.

Microsoft already gives users a handful of power profiles to choose from, but there's one option that isn't exposed in Windows 11's standard settings, and that's "Ultimate Performance." It may sound promising on paper, but it's only worthwhile if it makes a meaningful difference, which is exactly what I set out to find.

4 reasons why I paid for Windows 11 Pro and why I'll never switch to Linux

It's not you, Penguin, it's the industry around you

16
By  Abhinav Raj

The different Windows power plans tweak tiny aspects of your system

Most of the changes a plan makes lie in the CPU

When you change Windows 11 power plan, the bulk of the changes come from the CPU's behavior. Power plans change how aggressively (or not) Windows manages power, wakes up processor cores, and responds to sudden workloads. By default, the "Balanced" power plan is absolutely more than enough for the bulk of users, and yes, that includes gamers running heavy AAA games. However, that doesn't mean that High or even the Ultimate power plans don't do anything at all.

The first distinction is processor performance scaling. On my system, Balanced allows more conservative scaling, while the performance-oriented plans permit the CPU to reach its full advertised 4.4GHz boost when needed. Minimum processor state is another matter: Balanced can drop to 0%, while Ultimate Performance keeps it at 100%. That doesn't mean your CPU consumes maximum power constantly, but it does reduce its freedom to downclock at idle.

Another crucial area of importance here is core parking. The Balanced plan waits until individual cores reach roughly 80% utilization before it lets the CPU unpark more cores, while the higher performance-focused plans bring that threshold down to around 65%, unparking cores quicker. They also tend to keep awakened cores available for longer, rather than parking them as soon as demand subsides. Obviously, the "Ultimate" performance plan disables core parking entirely, making the processor ready to go at a moment's notice.

I had Claude look into my Windows 11 PC, and it revealed problems I didn’t know I had

"Hey Claude, what's wrong with my PC?"

3
By  Abhinav Raj

The Ultimate Performance power plan is easy to unlock

A simple command line takes the shackles off the CPU

In order to unlock the "Ultimate Performance" power plan in your Power Options menu, you must first open Command Prompt. Run an elevated CMD by choosing to run it as administrator from the Start Menu, and input the following line of code into it:

powercfg -duplicatescheme e9a42b02-d5df-448d-aa00-03f14749eb61

With that done, simply reopen the Power Options settings in the Control Panel, and right beside Balanced and High Performance, you should now also see a power plan titled "Ultimate Performance." This is the High Performance with its gloves off.

You can even click on Change plan settings > Change advanced power settings to tweak individual aspects of the CPU behavior and other efficiency options, turning them on or off to customize your Ultimate power plan to your needs.

The Ultimate Performance plan is really meant for workstations, but it does have some real uses for those who work with large files and video editing software. Since the CPU goes from intense workloads to an idle state more frequently for such users, keeping the CPU active and pinned at maximum performance really does save a precious couple of seconds every time.

On the other hand, the Ultimate Performance power plan truly doesn't do much for gamers. You might notice a few quicker boots and loads, but outside of that, every performance difference mostly falls within the margin for error.

This power plan favors consistency over efficiency, pushing your CPU to stay alert rather than to merely sip power. In practice, it increases heat and idle consumption, but it does ensure the processor is always ready to deliver maximum performance the instant a demanding workload kicks in.

3 reasons single-core CPU performance is still important

More cores don't always lead to a better CPU.

2
By  Rich Edmonds

Gaming performance remained largely unchanged

Everything within the margin of error

  • Credit: CD Projekt RED
  • Credit: CD Projekt RED

With the Ultimate Performance power plan turned on, I tested four of the games I play the most on a weekly, if not daily basis. Between the four of them, I get all sorts of scenarios vis-à-vis CPU-bound and GPU-bound workloads. Fortnite and Cyberpunk 2077 are more CPU-bound titles out of the four, while the other remain GPU-heavy.

Fortnite was the only one where I actually saw any real benefit to the Ultimate Performance power plan. My 1% lows improved remarkably in Fortnite after turning off all power-saving features through my power plan, but in the rest of the games, nothing changed all that much.

Three out of the four games support DLSS Frame Generation, but I chose not to use that setting as it takes even more load off the CPU. This helped me see more clearly whether removing the idle power settings from the CPU helped overall performance. The result, sadly, was rather unimpressive in all three titles. Ultimate Performance really isn't for everyone
